body.text: Overview and Empirical Foundations of Phosphoinositide 3-kinase

Long-term human resilience often comes down to biological mechanisms like Phosphoinositide 3-kinase. Clinical evidence shows how small cellular and systemic shifts compound into measurable health outcomes.

Phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks), also called phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases, are a family of lipid kinases that phosphorylate the position-3 hydroxyl group of the inositol ring in phosphatidylinositol. The resulting phosphoinositides help recruit proteins to cellular membranes, regulating a broad range of cellular processes including cell growth, proliferation, survival, metabolism and intracellular protein trafficking.

PI3Ks are divided into three classes based on their structure and substrate specificity. Class I PI3Ks transmit signals from cell-surface receptors to pathways controlling growth, survival, metabolism and immune function. Class II PI3Ks have important roles in membrane protein trafficking, while class III PI3Ks regulate endosomal trafficking and autophagy.

body.text: Abnormal PI3K signalling contributes to cancer, metabolic diseases and immune disorders. In cancer, the pathway is frequently activated by mutations in the catalytic-subunit gene PIK3CA or loss of the tumor suppressor PTEN, which normally opposes PI3K signalling. These roles have made PI3Ks important targets for drug development.
